summary:
Researched 2026-10-09 against systemd man pages and source (main, v252), the raspberrypi/utils pinctrl source, OctoPrint and OctoPi source, the Python docs, the Raspberry Pi release notes and news, the 2026-10-06 Pi OS Lite package lists, and GitHub, gh and actions/attest sources.

Supervision: with Restart=on-failure, ExecStopPost= runs after every kind of stop. That covers a crash exit, SIGKILL, a watchdog abort and a failed start. It always runs before the restart, and its timeout is TimeoutStopSec= (default 90 s). In a crash loop the start limit is checked at the next start, before any process is spawned. The last ExecStopPost has therefore already run, and the unit ends up 'failed' (start-limit-hit). The defaults (100 ms RestartSec, 5 starts per 10 s) reach that within about half a second.
Hang detection needs no dependency. systemd's sd_notify(3) ships a self-contained MIT-0 Python example, about 10 lines of AF_UNIX datagram code. Send the pings from the asyncio loop, gated on control-loop liveness.
pinctrl works without root if it can open /dev/gpiomem* (gpio group). Otherwise it falls back to /dev/mem, which needs root. The '+' prefix runs it as root regardless, but it does not bypass DevicePolicy=. Two caveats: Trixie (systemd 257) fires OnFailure= on every crash, Bookworm (252) does not; and Restart=on-failure does not restart after a clean SIGTERM exit.

Self-update: OctoPrint pip-installs a GitHub source zip in place into its running venv, without a checksum or rollback, then runs a configured restart command. OctoPi makes that work with a broad sudoers rule ('pi ALL=NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/service'). OctoPrint also queues updates while printing, refuses them when the Pi is throttled or low on disk, and sits behind a login. None of that login protection applies to BrewberryPi (IF-060).
A Python minor-version change (Bookworm 3.11 to Trixie 3.13) breaks venvs; Python says to recreate them.
Pi OS Lite 2026-10-06 (armhf and arm64) preinstalls python3-gpiozero, python3-lgpio, polkitd 126, sudo, gpgv, sqv, openssl 3.5 and python3-cryptography. So a pure-Python app wheel plus a --system-site-packages venv avoids native wheels, and a root updater can verify signatures without installing anything.
Passwordless sudo is off on new images since 2026-04-13 (not on upgraded installs). That breaks only unattended sudo through the login user, not a systemd-triggered updater.

Recommended design:
- The app writes only a request flag. A .path unit starts a root oneshot in its own cgroup (polkit is the equivalent alternative; sudo is worse because NoNewPrivileges= blocks it and it runs in the app's cgroup).
- The oneshot downloads from a hard-coded GitHub URL, verifies a signature with a pinned key (SHA-256 alone proves only integrity), installs into a new side-by-side venv, flips the 'current' symlink, then restarts the app and health-checks it (READY=1, /health, a stability window). On failure it rolls back.
- The app refuses updates in Loaded, Running or Paused, rate-limits requests, and validates Origin and Host, because without authentication any web page opened on the LAN could trigger the update.
GitHub artifact attestations are free for public repos and verifiable offline with a bundle, but Debian's gh 2.46 lacks 'gh attestation'. Treat attestation as optional.

claims.claim: With Restart=on-failure, systemd runs ExecStopPost= on every termination path: the main process exits non-zero, is killed by any signal (including SIGKILL / kill -9), is aborted by the watchdog, or the service fails during start-up. The commands get $SERVICE_RESULT (e.g. exit-code, signal, core-dump, watchdog, timeout), $EXIT_CODE and $EXIT_STATUS, so the reset helper can log the cause. ExecStopPost does not run on power loss, a kernel panic or a PID 1 crash.
claims.evidence: systemd.service(5) ExecStopPost=: 'Additional commands that are executed after the service is stopped. This includes cases where the commands configured in ExecStop= were used, where the service does not have any ExecStop= defined, or where the service exited unexpectedly ... unlike ExecStop= – commands specified with this setting are invoked when a service failed to start up correctly' (https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/systemd.service.xml). Source flow, src/core/service.c (main): service_enter_running() with result != SUCCESS -> service_enter_signal(SERVICE_STOP_SIGTERM) -> ... -> service_enter_stop_post() spawns exec_command[SERVICE_EXEC_STOP_POST]. The watchdog path (service_dispatch_watchdog / service_force_watchdog) calls service_enter_signal(s, SERVICE_STOP_WATCHDOG, SERVICE_FAILURE_WATCHDOG), which also ends in service_enter_stop_post(). systemd v252 (Bookworm) has the same stop_post calls (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/systemd/systemd/v252/src/core/service.c). systemd.exec(5) $SERVICE_RESULT: 'passed to all ExecStop= and ExecStopPost= processes' with values success|protocol|timeout|exit-code|signal|core-dump|watchdog|exec-condition|oom-kill|start-limit-hit|resources.

claims.claim:
Order after an unexpected main-process death:
1. ExecStop= runs, if one is configured.
2. Leftover processes in the unit's cgroup get SIGTERM (KillMode=control-group), then SIGKILL after TimeoutStopSec=.
3. ExecStopPost= runs.
4. Final SIGTERM/SIGKILL of anything left.
5. The unit enters failed-before-auto-restart / auto-restart.
6. RestartSec= (default 100 ms) elapses.
7. A new start job is queued; it runs the start-limit check, then ExecStartPre=.
So the GPIO reset always finishes (or times out) before the next instance starts.

Timeouts:
- ExecStopPost uses TimeoutStopSec= (default DefaultTimeoutStopSec=90 s). On timeout, TimeoutStopFailureMode= (default terminate) sends SIGTERM to it and the result becomes 'timeout'.
- A watchdog stop first sends WatchdogSignal= (default SIGABRT) and waits TimeoutAbortSec= (defaults to TimeoutStopSec=) before SIGKILL.

Recommendation: set short TimeoutAbortSec= and TimeoutStopSec= (e.g. 5–10 s). A hung process that froze with the heater ON keeps it ON until the reset runs.
claims.evidence: src/core/service.c (main): service_enter_stop_post() calls service_spawn(..., s->timeout_stop_usec, ...) and then sets SERVICE_STOP_POST. Its timer handler for SERVICE_STOP_POST logs "State 'stop-post' timed out. Terminating." and calls service_enter_signal(SERVICE_FINAL_SIGTERM, SERVICE_FAILURE_TIMEOUT). service_enter_signal() uses service_timeout_abort_usec(s) for KILL_WATCHDOG and timeout_stop_usec otherwise. service_enter_dead() arms the restart timer (RestartSec) only after the stop-post/final-kill states. service_enter_restart() queues the JOB_START. systemd.service(5): 'RestartSec= ... Defaults to 100ms'. systemd-system.conf(5): 'DefaultTimeoutAbortSec= is not set by default so that all units fall back to TimeoutStopSec='. TimeoutStopFailureMode= was added in v246 and TimeoutAbortSec= in v243 (version-info in systemd.service.xml), so both work on Bookworm (252) and Trixie (257).

claims.claim:
What Restart=on-failure restarts:
- It restarts after a non-zero exit, an 'unclean' signal (SIGKILL, SIGABRT, SIGSEGV, ...), a timeout, or a watchdog expiry.
- It does NOT restart after exit 0 or after death by SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGPIPE.

Consequence: NFR-022 makes the app exit cleanly on SIGTERM. A stray `kill <pid>` from outside systemd therefore leaves the controller stopped (outputs reset by ExecStopPost, but no restart). Restart=always would also restart in that case, and still not after `systemctl stop`.
claims.evidence: systemd.service(5) Restart=: 'a clean exit means ... exit code of 0; for types other than Type=oneshot, one of the signals SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGTERM, or SIGPIPE' and 'If set to on-failure, the service will be restarted when the process exits with a non-zero exit code, is terminated by a signal (including on core dump, but excluding the aforementioned four signals), when an operation ... times out, and when the configured watchdog timeout is triggered'. Also: 'the service will not be restarted if ... the service is stopped with systemctl stop'. service.c service_shall_restart(): SERVICE_RESTART_ON_FAILURE returns !IN_SET(result, SERVICE_SUCCESS, SERVICE_SKIP_CONDITION).

claims.claim:
How the systemd watchdog works:
- It needs WatchdogSec= in the unit and a periodic sd_notify 'WATCHDOG=1' from the app. If the pings stop, systemd marks the unit failed (result 'watchdog') and kills it with SIGABRT. Restart=on-failure (or on-watchdog / on-abnormal / always) then restarts it, after ExecStopPost has run.
- systemd passes WATCHDOG_USEC and WATCHDOG_PID to the app. sd_watchdog_enabled(3) recommends pinging 'every half of the time'.
- The watchdog only starts after start-up completes (READY=1 with Type=notify). Hangs during start-up are caught by TimeoutStartSec=.
- 'WATCHDOG=trigger' lets the app request the watchdog action itself, for example when it detects a stuck sensor or control loop.

Python detail: SIGABRT kills a Python process at once unless a handler is installed. faulthandler (PYTHONFAULTHANDLER=1) dumps the tracebacks of the hung threads to the journal first.
claims.evidence: systemd.service(5) WatchdogSec=: 'The watchdog is activated when the start-up is completed. The service must call sd_notify(3) regularly with WATCHDOG=1 ... If the time between two such calls is larger than the configured time, then the service is placed in a failed state and it will be terminated with SIGABRT (or the signal specified by WatchdogSignal=). By setting Restart= to on-failure, on-watchdog, on-abnormal or always, the service will be automatically restarted. The time configured here will be passed to the executed service process in the WATCHDOG_USEC= environment variable.' sd_watchdog_enabled(3): 'keep-alive notification message to the service manager every half of the time returned here'; the call 'will ignore these variables if $WATCHDOG_PID does not contain the PID of the current process'. sd_notify(3) WATCHDOG=trigger: 'Tells the service manager that the service detected an internal error that should be handled by the configured watchdog options.' (https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/sd_notify.xml). The faulthandler point is from the Python docs from memory and was not re-fetched here.

sd_notify(3) section 'Standalone Implementations': 'it is also possible to reimplement the simple readiness notification protocol without external dependencies, as demonstrated in the following self-contained examples'. It includes man/notify-selfcontained-example.py (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/systemd/systemd/main/man/notify-selfcontained-example.py): '# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT-0 ... # This protocol is guaranteed to be stable as per: https://systemd.io/PORTABILITY_AND_STABILITY/', with code: socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_DGRAM | socket.SOCK_CLOEXEC); sock.connect(socket_path); sock.sendall(message); and abstract handling `if socket_path[0] == '@': socket_path = '\0' + socket_path[1:]`. sd_notify(3) Notes: 'If the first character of $NOTIFY_SOCKET is / or @, the string is understood as an AF_UNIX or Linux abstract namespace socket'.

claims.claim: NotifyAccess= takes none (the default), main, exec or all. With Type=notify or WatchdogSec= and no explicit setting, it is implicitly 'main', so only the main PID's datagrams are accepted. ExecStart= must therefore start the Python process directly, or through a wrapper that uses `exec`. Use exec or all only if a child process sends the pings. Messages from short-lived auxiliary processes can be dropped even with 'all'.
claims.evidence: systemd.service(5) NotifyAccess=: 'Takes one of none (the default), main, exec or all ... If main, only service updates sent from the main process of the service are accepted ... If those options are used but NotifyAccess= is not configured, it will be implicitly set to main' and 'if an auxiliary process of the unit sends an sd_notify() message and immediately exits, the service manager might not be able to properly attribute the message to the unit, and thus will ignore it, even if NotifyAccess=all is set'.

claims.claim:
Crash loops and the start limit:
- Defaults are StartLimitBurst=5 per StartLimitIntervalSec=10 s and RestartSec=100 ms, so a crash-on-start loop hits the limit in well under a second.
- The limit is tested at the next start attempt, before any process (including ExecStartPre) is spawned. The unit then enters 'failed' with result 'start-limit-hit' and is not restarted automatically any more. It can be started manually or by a timer after the interval; `systemctl reset-failed` clears the counter.
- ExecStopPost runs after every crash in the loop, because it runs before each restart (G02). The final state is therefore 'failed' with outputs as the last ExecStopPost left them (off).
- StartLimitAction= defaults to none.
- StartLimitIntervalSec=/StartLimitBurst= go in [Unit], not [Service].
- RestartSteps= / RestartMaxDelaySec= (exponential back-off) need systemd >= 254: available on Trixie (257), not on Bookworm (252).

Recommendation: RestartSec=2–5 s, and size the limits so that a slow-booting Pi 3 does not trip them.
claims.evidence: systemd.unit(5) StartLimitIntervalSec=/StartLimitBurst=: 'Units which are started more than burst times within an interval time span are not permitted to start any more ... units which are configured for Restart=, and which reach the start limit are not attempted to be restarted anymore; however, they may still be restarted manually or from a timer or socket at a later point, after the interval has passed ... systemctl reset-failed will cause the restart rate counter for a service to be flushed'. systemd-system.conf(5): 'DefaultStartLimitIntervalSec= defaults to 10s. DefaultStartLimitBurst= defaults to 5.' service.c service_test_startable(): `r = unit_test_start_limit(u); if (r < 0) { service_enter_dead(s, SERVICE_FAILURE_START_LIMIT_HIT, false); ...}`, which runs before service_start() spawns anything. StartLimitAction=: 'Defaults to none'. RestartSteps=/RestartMaxDelaySec= are tagged version 254 in systemd.service.xml. Lite 2026-10-06 ships systemd 257.13 (arm64) / 257.9+rpi1 (armhf).

claims.claim:
OnFailure= behaves differently on Bookworm and Trixie:
- systemd >= 254 (Trixie 257): with the default RestartMode=normal, every failure passes through the transitional state 'failed-before-auto-restart', which maps to UNIT_FAILED. An OnFailure= unit (alarm, rollback) therefore fires on EVERY crash, even ones that are auto-restarted. RestartMode=direct (>= 254) suppresses this until the state has converged.
- systemd 252 (Bookworm): auto-restart maps to 'activating', so OnFailure= fires only on the final failure.
A rollback or alarm hook built on OnFailure= must account for this.
claims.evidence: service.c (main) state table: `[SERVICE_FAILED_BEFORE_AUTO_RESTART] = UNIT_FAILED`. unit.c: `else if (ns != os && ns == UNIT_FAILED) unit_start_on_termination_deps(u, UNIT_ATOM_ON_FAILURE);`. service_enter_dead() comment: 'so that external software can watch the state changes and see all service failures, even if they are only transitionary and followed by an automatic restart'. NEWS 254: 'RestartMode= which can be set to direct ... this means that OnSuccess=/OnFailure= units will not be triggered until the service state has converged'. v252 service.c: `[SERVICE_AUTO_RESTART] = UNIT_ACTIVATING` and no FAILED_BEFORE_AUTO_RESTART state. NEWS 239: OnFailure units 'will no longer be triggered on failures that result in restarting'. That was the behaviour until 254.

claims.claim:
Running pinctrl in ExecStopPost under User=brewberrypi:

Without '+':
- pinctrl reads the device tree from /sys/firmware/devicetree/base (world-readable) and /sys/bus/gpio/devices.
- It then opens /dev/gpiomem<N> for each memory-mapped GPIO chip found through the DT gpio aliases. For any chip whose gpiomem node cannot be opened, it falls back to /dev/mem (root only) and aborts with 'Must be root (or group 'gpio' on RPiOS)'.
- On Raspberry Pi OS, /dev/gpiomem* are root:gpio 0660 (hardware claim C08). A service user in the gpio group can therefore run it, provided every gpiomem node pinctrl needs exists and is accessible. On a Pi 5 that may be several nodes (gpiomem0..N); untested here.

With '+':
- '+' runs the command as root, ignoring User=, Group=, SupplementaryGroups= and namespacing options such as PrivateDevices=.
- It does NOT bypass cgroup-wide settings such as DevicePolicy=/DeviceAllow=. Restricting devices for the app therefore also restricts the reset unless /dev/gpiomem* is allowed.

Recommendation:
- Use `ExecStopPost=+/usr/bin/pinctrl set 22,23 op dh` plus `pinctrl set 10 op dl` for the buzzer. It is a fixed command with no input, so running it as root costs little and removes the dependency on group membership.
- Optionally add the same command as ExecStartPre=+, to drive the outputs off before Python starts. This matters on a slow Pi 3.
- pinctrl is a system binary, independent of the venv, so the reset still works when the venv is broken (G13).
claims.evidence: raspberrypi/utils pinctrl/gpiolib.c (master): gpio_add_chip_instance(): `sprintf(pathbuf, "/dev/gpiomem%s", gpiomem_idx); inst->mem_fd = open(pathbuf, O_RDWR|O_SYNC);`. gpiolib_init(): `const char *dtpath = "/sys/firmware/devicetree/base"` and alias scan `gpio%d`. In the mmap loop: `if (inst->mem_fd >= 0) mmap(...) else { mem_fd = open("/dev/mem", O_RDWR|O_SYNC); if (mem_fd < 0) return errno; }`. pinctrl.c: `if (ret == EACCES && geteuid()) printf("Must be root (or group 'gpio' on RPiOS)\n");`. systemd.service(5) prefix table: '+ ... privilege restrictions configured with User=, Group=, CapabilityBoundingSet= or the various file system namespacing options (such as PrivateDevices=, PrivateTmp=) are not applied ... However, note that this will not bypass options that apply to the whole control group, such as DevicePolicy='. systemd.exec(5) SupplementaryGroups=: 'This does not affect commands prefixed with +'.

claims.claim:
An updater started as a child of the app process lives in the app's cgroup. Examples: subprocess pip followed by `sudo systemctl restart`, or `sudo some-script`. When the app unit stops or restarts, systemd kills every remaining process in that cgroup (KillMode=control-group, the default), so such an updater can kill itself halfway through an install.

OctoPrint gets away with it because the restart is the last step and `service ... restart` only queues a job in PID 1. For BrewberryPi the privileged update work must run in its own unit, for example a oneshot started via a .path unit or via polkit-authorised StartUnit(). Then PID 1 owns it and restarting the app cannot kill it.
claims.evidence: systemd.kill(5) KillMode=: 'If set to control-group, all remaining processes in the control group of this unit will be killed on unit stop (for services: after the stop command is executed, as configured with ExecStop=)'. OctoPrint su_init.py: the update finishes with _perform_restart() -> self._system_commands.perform_server_restart() (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctoPrint/OctoPrint/master/src/octoprint/plugins/softwareupdate/__init__.py).

claims.claim:
How OctoPrint's Software Update plugin updates and restarts (the precedent):
- The 'pip' method runs `pip install <URL>` inside OctoPrint's own running venv, in place. OctoPrint's own default check is type github_release with pip URL 'https://github.com/OctoPrint/OctoPrint/archive/{target_version}.zip', a GitHub source archive. The docs and the update path show no checksum or signature verification, and I found no rollback/revert code in the plugin.
- Restart uses the configured server.commands.serverRestartCommand. OctoPi sets 'serverRestartCommand: sudo service octoprint restart' and 'systemRestartCommand: sudo shutdown -r now'. It installs sudoers rules '${BASE_USER} ALL=NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/service' and '/sbin/shutdown'. The service rule lets the user start or stop ANY service as root.
- OctoPrint's update API sits behind its login and permission system (Permissions.PLUGIN_SOFTWAREUPDATE_UPDATE). BrewberryPi has no equivalent (IF-060).
claims.evidence: https://docs.octoprint.org/en/master/bundledplugins/softwareupdate.html: pip method 'Update by pip install'ing the supplied URL'; 'Restart commands for OctoPrint and the whole server can be configured under Settings > Server'. Source su_init.py: default check `"method": "pip", "pip": "https://github.com/OctoPrint/OctoPrint/archive/{target_version}.zip", "restart": "octoprint"`, VALID_RESTART_TYPES = ("octoprint", "environment"), perform_update() begins with `if not Permissions.PLUGIN_SOFTWAREUPDATE_UPDATE.can() ...: flask.abort(403)`. grep for rollback/revert in __init__.py and updaters/pip.py: no matches. OctoPi https://raw.githubusercontent.com/guysoft/OctoPi/devel/src/modules/octopi/start_chroot_script lines 210-211: `echo "${BASE_USER} ALL=NOPASSWD: /sbin/shutdown" > /etc/sudoers.d/octoprint-shutdown`, `echo "${BASE_USER} ALL=NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/service" > /etc/sudoers.d/octoprint-service`. OctoPi config.yaml (filesystem/home/pi/.octoprint/config.yaml): `serverRestartCommand: sudo service octoprint restart`.

claims.claim:
OctoPrint's guards and failure modes:
- It refuses an update with HTTP 409 when the Pi is currently throttled ('System is currently throttled, refusing to update anything due to possible stability issues'), with the warning that updating anyway may 'outright corrupt your install'.
- It refuses when the environment is unsupported (Python < 3.7, setuptools < 40.8 or pip < 20.3: 'Direct updates are not supported in this Python environment') and when free disk space is below minimum_free_storage (default 150 MB).
- While a print is running or paused it does not refuse: it QUEUES the update targets and runs them after the print.
- Documented failure outcomes: a pip failure becomes UpdateError ('Error while executing pip install'). A failing restart command becomes RestartFailed, with its stdout and stderr logged. The event plugin_softwareupdate_update_failed is fired.
These are good precedents for BrewberryPi: refuse when throttled, low on disk or not idle.
claims.evidence: su_init.py perform_update(): throttle check with flask.abort(409, ...); `if not self._environment_supported: flask.abort(409, description="Direct updates are not supported in this Python environment")`; `if not self._storage_sufficient: flask.abort(409, description="Not enough free disk space for updating")`; `if self._printer.is_printing() or self._printer.is_paused(): # do not update while a print job is running # store targets to be run later on print done event`. MINIMUM_PYTHON="3.7", MINIMUM_SETUPTOOLS="40.8", MINIMUM_PIP="20.3"; defaults 'ignore_throttled': False, 'minimum_free_storage': 150; the ignore_throttled log warning text. updaters/pip.py raises exceptions.UpdateError("Error while executing pip install", ...). _perform_restart() raises exceptions.RestartFailed() and logs the restart stdout/stderr.

claims.claim:
A Python minor-version change breaks a venv, and in-place OS upgrades cause exactly that. Pi OS Bookworm ships 3.11 and Trixie 3.13 (OS-02).
- After an in-place dist-upgrade the venv's interpreter links resolve to the new python3, but its packages are in lib/python3.11/site-packages, and compiled extensions are cp311. Imports fail and the service crash-loops into start-limit-hit (G07); ExecStopPost still resets the pins each time.
- Python's docs say venvs are 'Not considered as movable or copyable -- you just recreate the same environment'. `venv --upgrade` only re-points the interpreter, 'assuming Python has been upgraded in-place'.
- OctoPrint users hit this repeatedly (e.g. Buster to Bullseye), and OctoPrint offers octoprint-venv-tool 'recreate-venv' or 'reflash + restore backup'.
- Raspberry Pi itself recommends a clean install over in-place upgrades (OS-05).

Mitigations:
- An installer or ExecStartPre= check compares pyvenv.cfg 'version' with the system python3 and rebuilds the venv from a locally cached wheel when they differ.
- Keep the GPIO reset outside the venv (G09).
claims.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/main/Doc/library/venv.rst: '* Not considered as movable or copyable -- you just recreate the same environment in the target location.'; '--upgrade  Upgrade the environment directory to use this version of Python, assuming Python has been upgraded in-place.'; 'environments are inherently non-portable, in the general case. You should always have a simple means of recreating an environment'. OctoPrint community threads, found by search; the pages themselves are behind Anubis bot protection, so I could not fetch them: https://community.octoprint.org/t/pios-bullseye-killed-octoprint/38790 , https://community.octoprint.org/t/61076 (FAQ: './octoprint-venv-tool recreate-venv /home/pi/oprint --python ...'), https://community.octoprint.org/t/octoprint-service-died-after-apt-upgrade/24044 . The crash-loop consequence is inferred from G07, not tested.

https://downloads.raspberrypi.com/raspios_lite_arm64/images/raspios_lite_arm64-2026-10-06/2026-10-06-raspios-trixie-arm64-lite.info and .../raspios_lite_armhf-2026-10-06/2026-10-06-raspios-trixie-armhf-lite.info (dpkg lists): 'ii  python3-gpiozero 2.0.1-0+rpt1+trixie', 'ii  python3-lgpio 0.2.2-1~rpt1+trixie', 'ii  python3-libgpiod 2.2.1-2+deb13u1' (armhf: 2.2.1-2+rpi1+deb13u1), 'ii  polkitd 126-2', 'ii  sudo 1.9.16p2-3+deb13u2', 'ii  gpgv 2.4.7-21+deb13u1', 'ii  sqv 1.3.0-3', 'ii  openssl 3.5.7-1~deb13u3+rpt1', 'ii  python3-cryptography 43.0.0-3+deb13u1', 'ii  python3-venv 3.13.5-1' (arm64), 'ii  systemd 257.13-1~deb13u1' (arm64) / '257.9-1~deb13u1+rpi1' (armhf).

claims.claim:
Passwordless sudo, verified:
- The Raspberry Pi OS release notes for 2026-04-13 say 'Passwordless sudo now disabled by default', and add a switch in Control Centre and raspi-config to turn it back on.
- Raspberry Pi's announcement (14 April 2026, Raspberry Pi OS 6.2) says this 'will not affect updates to existing installations'. Only NEW images are affected. After a password is entered, sudo does not prompt again for five minutes.

Effect on BrewberryPi:
- An interactive installer run with sudo still works (one password prompt).
- Unattended installs through the login user break: non-tty SSH, `curl | sudo bash`, Ansible without a become password.
- An updater must never rely on the login user's sudo. It is unaffected if it runs as a root systemd unit (.path or polkit trigger) or through a dedicated sudoers rule for the service user, which the installer writes once.
claims.evidence: https://downloads.raspberrypi.com/raspios_lite_arm64/release_notes.txt: '2026-04-13: * Passwordless sudo now disabled by default * Switch to enable passwordless sudo added to Control Centre System tab and to raspi-config'. https://www.raspberrypi.com/news/a-security-update-for-raspberry-pi-os/ (datePublished 14 April 2026): 'passwordless sudo is now disabled by default'; 'this change will not affect updates to existing installations of Raspberry Pi OS'; 'you won't be prompted again for the next five minutes'. Extends runtime claim OS-06.

claims.claim:
Recommended privilege boundary: the app never runs privileged code. It only writes a request flag (e.g. /var/lib/brewberrypi/update/request) in a directory it owns. A root brewberrypi-update.path unit (PathExists=) starts a Type=oneshot brewberrypi-update.service.

systemd caveats:
- When the triggered service ends, the path is re-checked immediately and the service starts again at once if the flag still exists. The oneshot must therefore delete or rename the flag first.
- If the oneshot hits its start limit, the failure propagates to the path unit, which fails and stops watching until restarted or rebooted.
- The path unit's own trigger limit defaults to 200 activations per 2 s.
- The updater must treat the flag's contents as untrusted: no URL or path from it, at most a version string checked against the signed manifest.

Alternatives:
- polkit: systemd checks org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units with the details 'unit' and 'verb' (since v226). A /etc/polkit-1/rules.d rule can allow user brewberrypi to 'start' exactly brewberrypi-update.service. polkitd is preinstalled (G14). It also works under NoNewPrivileges=yes, because it is IPC.
- sudoers: an exact rule such as 'brewberrypi ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl start brewberrypi-update.service'. sudo is setuid, so it fails under NoNewPrivileges=yes (and settings that imply it). Running the update itself under sudo would also put it in the app's cgroup (G10).

Verdict: .path is simplest (no D-Bus or polkit dependency, nothing setuid). polkit is equivalent and gives immediate feedback. sudoers is the weakest.
claims.evidence: systemd.path(5): 'When a service unit triggered by a path unit terminates (regardless whether it exited successfully or failed), monitored paths are checked immediately again, and the service accordingly restarted instantly. As protection against busy looping ... a start rate limit is enforced on the service unit ... the error condition that the start rate limit is hit is propagated from the service unit to the path unit and causes the path unit to fail as well, thus ending the loop.' TriggerLimitIntervalSec= 'defaults to 2s', TriggerLimitBurst= 'defaults to 200 ... If the limit is hit, the unit is placed into a failure mode, and will not watch the paths anymore until restarted'. 'PathExists= may be used to watch the mere existence of a file'. org.freedesktop.systemd1(5) Security: 'Operations which modify unit state (StartUnit(), StopUnit() ... RestartUnit() ...) require org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units'. NEWS 226: 'When systemd requests a polkit decision when managing units it will now add additional fields to the request, including unit name and desired operation'. src/core/dbus-util.c: details 'unit', 'verb'. systemd.exec(5) NoNewPrivileges=: 'can never gain new privileges through execve() (e.g. via setuid or setgid bits ...)' and 'It has no effect on processes potentially invoked on request of them through tools such as ... systemd-run, or arbitrary IPC services'.

claims.claim:
Proposed update transaction (my design, built from the facts above):
1. Download from a hard-coded release URL: a pure-Python wheel, its SHA-256 and a detached signature.
2. Verify the signature with a pinned key.
3. Build a new venv side by side, /opt/brewberrypi/releases/<ver>/venv (--system-site-packages). Install the app wheel and its pinned pure-Python dependencies with `pip install --no-index` from a verified wheelhouse. Alternatively, install from PyPI with a hash-pinned requirements file (`--require-hashes`) that is covered by the signature.
4. Atomically flip /opt/brewberrypi/current: symlink to a temp name, then rename(2) via `mv -T`.
5. Run `systemctl reset-failed brewberrypi` and `systemctl restart brewberrypi`, without --no-block. With Type=notify the job completes only on READY=1 and fails if the app dies first.
6. Health check: probe http://127.0.0.1:8080/health, which reports that engine, HAL and sensor are initialised, then require a stability window of e.g. 60 s with ActiveState=active and NRestarts unchanged.
7. On any failure: flip the symlink back, restart, record the version as bad so it is not retried automatically, and report through a status file the UI reads.
Keep the previous release (N=2) for rollback.

This mirrors podman auto-update's rollback (PODMAN-04), but systemd has no built-in rollback for native installs. Do not build rollback on OnFailure= alone (G08).
claims.evidence: Derived from G02, G04, G07, G08, G10 and G16. Restart counter: service.c service_enter_restart() 'restart counter is at %u' (n_restarts, exposed as the NRestarts property). Type=notify readiness: systemd.service(5) (the Type= text was not re-quoted here). Podman's rollback: runtime claim PODMAN-04.

claims.claim:
Checksums and signatures:
- A SHA-256 file fetched from the same GitHub Release only detects corruption or truncation. Anyone who can replace the asset (a compromised account or token) can replace the checksum too. Authenticity needs a signature checked against a key pinned in the INSTALLED version: minisign/signify Ed25519, or OpenPGP checked with gpgv/sqv.
- Tools: gpgv, sqv and openssl 3.5 are already on Lite (G14). minisign 0.12 and signify-openbsd are in Debian trixie for armhf and arm64.
- The Python stdlib has no Ed25519, so in-app verification would need `cryptography`. python3-cryptography 43 is on Lite.
claims.evidence: Package lists in G14. Debian madison (https://api.ftp-master.debian.org/madison?package=minisign): 'minisign | 0.12-1 | stable | source, amd64, arm64, armel, armhf ...'; signify-openbsd 32-1.1 stable (armhf, arm64). The stdlib point is from general knowledge: hashlib/hmac only, no public-key signatures.

claims.claim:
GitHub artifact attestations (Sigstore) can be used on a Pi, with caveats:
- Free on public repos for all GitHub plans; private repos need Enterprise Cloud. Public repos use the Sigstore Public Good instance.
- actions/attest@v4 (permissions id-token: write, attestations: write, contents: read) outputs 'bundle-path', which can be uploaded as a release asset.
- On the device, `gh attestation verify <wheel> --repo owner/repo --bundle <file>` skips gh's auth check. Without --bundle it fetches attestations through the GitHub API and needs gh auth.
- Offline verification also needs a trusted_root.jsonl. It has no built-in expiry, but Sigstore rotates key material 'a few times per year', so it must be refreshed.
- The `gh attestation` command does not exist in gh v2.46.0, which is Debian trixie's gh; it is present in v2.49.0. A Pi would need GitHub's own gh package or binary. cosign 2.5.0 is packaged in Debian trixie (armhf, arm64), but I did not test it against GitHub bundles.
- GitHub warns that attestations 'are not a guarantee that an artifact is secure'. They prove which repo and workflow built it.
Verdict: optional second factor. A pinned signing key (G18) is simpler and works offline.
claims.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/actions/attest/main/README.md: 'Artifact attestations are available in public repositories for all current GitHub plans' ... private repos 'must be on a GitHub Enterprise Cloud plan' ... 'NOT supported on GitHub Enterprise Server'; outputs table '`bundle-path` | Absolute path to the file containing the generated attestation'. https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/use-artifact-attestations/use-artifact-attestations (actions/attest@v4, permissions). https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/use-artifact-attestations/verify-attestations-offline: 'gh attestation trusted-root > trusted_root.jsonl'; 'verify ... --bundle ... --custom-trusted-root trusted_root.jsonl'; 'does not have a built-in expiration date'. cli/cli trunk pkg/cmd/attestation/verify/verify.go: `cmdutil.DisableAuthCheckFlag(verifyCmd.Flags().Lookup("bundle"))`. raw.githubusercontent.com/cli/cli/v2.46.0/pkg/cmd/attestation/attestation.go -> 404, v2.49.0 -> 200. madison: gh 2.46.0-3 (trixie), cosign 2.5.0-2+b4 (trixie: arm64, armhf). https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/artifact-attestations: 'artifact attestations are not a guarantee that an artifact is secure'.

claims.claim:
Fixed source, no uploads:
- The updater hard-codes the upstream, e.g. https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<asset> (manifest, wheel, sig).
- That URL pattern is documented and needs no GitHub API call, so it is not subject to the unauthenticated API limit of 60/h. It works only for uploaded release assets, not for source archives.
- The web request carries no URL, file or path. The server offers no upload endpoint at all: with IF-060 (no auth), an upload or arbitrary-URL endpoint would hand root code execution to anyone on the LAN.
- Downgrades: the manifest version must be greater than the installed one unless a local rollback is running. Otherwise an attacker could replay an old signed vulnerable release.
claims.evidence: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/linking-to-releases: 'To link directly to a download of your latest release asset that was manually uploaded, link to /owner/name/releases/latest/download/asset-name.zip'. The API limit is from the shared research instructions (60/h unauthenticated). The downgrade/replay point is design reasoning.

claims.claim:
Without authentication, 'trusted LAN' also means any web page opened in a browser on that LAN can reach the Pi. Possible attacks:
- cross-site POST (CSRF);
- cross-site WebSocket hijacking, because browsers do not apply same-origin rules to WebSocket;
- DNS rebinding.

Minimum protection for the update trigger, and for the existing heater and process commands:
- Reject WebSocket handshakes whose Origin is not the Pi's own origin (RFC 6455 SHOULD).
- Validate the Host header against the expected names or IPs, against DNS rebinding.
- Make the HTTP update trigger a non-simple request (JSON content type or a custom header) so that cross-origin calls need a CORS preflight the server never grants, or send it over the Origin-checked WebSocket.

Chrome's Local Network Access prompt is not a dependable mitigation: opt-in in Chrome 138 (June 2025), reportedly enforced from Chrome 142 according to a secondary source, and not in all browsers.
claims.evidence: RFC 6455 §10.2 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.txt): 'Servers that are not intended to process input from any web page but only for certain sites SHOULD verify the |Origin| field is an origin they expect. If the origin indicated is unacceptable to the server, then it SHOULD respond to the WebSocket handshake with a reply containing HTTP 403 Forbidden'. Chrome: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access (June 9, 2025, opt-in testing; purpose: CSRF against routers and devices on private networks). The 'enforced from 142' claim comes from a third-party blog (https://blog.openreplay.com/chrome-local-network-access-lna-permission/) and was not confirmed by Google.

claims.claim:
Refusing updates during a brew: the app accepts an update request only when the engine state is NoProcess. Whether Finished and Stopped also count as idle is a spec question. It refuses in Loaded, Running and Paused (ENG-001 states).

To close the gap between the check and the restart:
- On acceptance the app enters an 'update pending' lock that rejects load and start until the updater restarts it or a timeout clears the lock.
- The root updater re-checks a localhost state endpoint just before stopping the service, and aborts if the state is not idle.

Also refuse, as OctoPrint does, when:
- the Pi is throttled now (`vcgencmd get_throttled`, bit 'currently under-voltage'),
- free space is below a threshold,
- the clock is not synced. NTP matters for TLS validity on a Pi without an RTC; this last point is my inference.

Restarting through systemctl triggers NFR-022's graceful all-off, and ExecStopPost resets the pins anyway.

OctoPrint precedent: it queues updates while printing or paused rather than refusing.
claims.evidence: docs/specification/03-brew-process-engine.md ENG-001: 'Engine state is NoProcess when no process is loaded; otherwise it is the state of the loaded process (Loaded, Running, Paused, Stopped, Finished)'. OctoPrint su_init.py: `if self._printer.is_printing() or self._printer.is_paused(): # do not update while a print job is running` (queues) and the throttle/storage refusals (G12). docs/specification/10-non-functional-requirements.md NFR-022.

claims.claim:
Rate limiting in layers:
- App: single-flight, so only one check or install is in progress. Cooldowns, e.g. at most one 'check for update' per few minutes and one install attempt per 10–15 min. Reply with the remaining wait time.
- systemd backstops: StartLimitIntervalSec=/StartLimitBurst= on the oneshot, and TriggerLimitIntervalSec=/TriggerLimitBurst= on the .path unit.
- Caveat: if the oneshot hits its start limit, the path unit fails and stops watching until restarted, so the update button silently stops working. Choose systemd limits that normal use never reaches, and let the app surface 'updater unavailable' by querying the path unit's state (readable without privileges).
claims.evidence: systemd.path(5) quotes in G16 (start-limit propagation; TriggerLimit defaults 2s/200; 'will not watch the paths anymore until restarted'). systemd.unit(5) StartLimit quotes in G07. org.freedesktop.systemd1(5): 'Read access is generally granted to all clients'.

open_questions: The specification has no self-update requirement. Web-triggered update is new scope that interacts with IF-060/Q-10. It should be recorded with /spec-question before implementation.

Hardware test: does `sudo -u brewberrypi pinctrl set 22,23 op dh` work for a gpio-group user on Pi 3, Pi 4 AND Pi 5? On Pi 5, pinctrl opens one /dev/gpiomem<N> per DT gpio alias and falls back to /dev/mem (root only) for any that fail. If it fails, use ExecStopPost=+.
Which engine states count as idle for updates? NoProcess for sure; Finished and Stopped still show goal data (DOM) and might be in use.

Should cross-origin protection (Origin and Host checks on the WebSocket and HTTP) become a spec requirement for ALL commands, not just updates? Without it, any web page opened on a LAN browser can send heater and process commands (CSWSH).
Not researched: do the Bookworm 'legacy' Lite images also ship python3-gpiozero, python3-lgpio and polkitd? Do cosign and gh exist in the 32-bit Raspbian archive, which is separate from Debian armhf?

Not researched: a hardware watchdog (bcm2835-wdt via systemd RuntimeWatchdogSec=) for kernel or PID 1 hangs. ExecStopPost cannot cover those. After such a reboot the relays depend on boot-time pin defaults (hardware claims C28–C31).
Is a GitHub Release 'latest' redirect acceptable as the only update channel, or is a pinned channel or tag manifest wanted so that a pre-release cannot reach a brewing kettle?
